title: Rice Stem Borer: Deadhearts, Whiteheads and How to Stop Them
metaTitle: Rice Stem Borer: Deadhearts, Whiteheads and Control
metaDescription: The rice stem borer kills tillers as deadhearts and empty panicles as whiteheads. Learn the signs, the natural enemies and a safe order of control.
excerpt: The rice stem borer is a group of moths whose larvae tunnel inside the stem of palay. They cause deadhearts before flowering and whiteheads after it. This page shows the signs, the damage and what to do first, long before any spray.

heroImage.alt: A yellow stem borer moth, Scirpophaga incertulas, with the small black dot on each pale yellow wing
heroImage.credit: Sabarni Sarker, CC BY, via iNaturalist

blocks.text:
Six stem borer species attack rice in Asia. The yellow stem borer (Scirpophaga incertulas) and the white stem borer (Scirpophaga innotata) are the best known. The striped stem borer (Chilo suppressalis), the gold fringed, the dark headed and the pink stem borer complete the list. All of them are moth larvae that live and feed inside the stem.

PhilRice names stem borers among the five major rice insect pests of the country. Its 2026 warning expected heavy attacks in Bicol, Central Luzon and Northern Mindanao in the early months of that year. So every palay farmer should know the signs, because a borer can hurt the crop from seedling to maturity.

blocks.caption: Quick facts
rows: Scirpophaga incertulas, Scirpophaga innotata, Chilo suppressalis
Stems and tillers and panicles and ears
From seedling to maturity, with deadhearts before flowering and whiteheads after it.
Moths lay egg masses on the leaves, the young larvae bore into the stem, and the pest can survive in stubble and volunteer rice between crops.

blocks.text: How to Identify Rice Stem Borer

Pull the central shoot of a suspect tiller. If it comes out easily and the base is rotten or bored, you have a deadheart. Split the stem and look for the larva, tiny holes and frass, which is the powdery waste it leaves inside. Later, a panicle that is white and empty while the leaves are still green is a whitehead. Do not mix it up with the rice bug or with the rice whorl maggot, which only scrapes the leaves and does not tunnel the stem.

items: The central shoot dries up and pulls out easily, which is a deadheart.
A panicle turns white or pale and carries no filled grain, which is a whitehead.
Tiny holes appear on the stem, with frass inside the tissue.
Egg masses sit on the leaves of the seedbed and the young plants.
Larvae in small tubes made of leaf wrappings float on the water and attach themselves to tillers.

blocks.title: Do not confuse it with
blocks.text: Deadhearts can look like damage from the [rice whorl maggot](/pests/rice-whorl-maggot) or from the [rice black bug](/pests/rice-black-bug). Only the stem borer leaves a bored stem with frass and a larva inside.
How Rice Stem Borer Hurts Your Palay

Stem borers can destroy rice at any growth stage, from seedling to maturity. Deadhearts take away tillers that would have carried grain. Whiteheads take away the panicle itself, so the grain is lost completely.

We found no official percent yield loss for the Philippines, so we do not state one. Timing still matters. PhilRice notes that rice hit during the vegetative and tillering stages can still recover, while a whitehead after flowering is lost for good. For the spray decision, use the light trap and the egg jar test below. Count the deadhearts and whiteheads in each lot every week, write them in your notes and compare season with season.
How to Control Rice Stem Borer

items: Prepare the land well. Plow and flood the field, and remove stubble and volunteer rice so the larvae have nowhere to wait.
Plant at the same time as your neighbors. Synchronous planting with the right timing breaks the supply of tillers for the moths.

Check the seedlings before you pull them. If the leaves carry many egg masses, collect the eggs by hand before transplanting. Do not cut the leaf tops instead, because PhilRice warns that cut leaves let disease organisms in.
Handpick and destroy egg masses in the seedbed and at transplanting. Raise the irrigation water now and then to drown eggs laid on the lower part of the plant.
Split the nitrogen fertilizer into doses as recommended, and harvest at ground level so less stubble remains.

Protect the natural enemies. Many wasps, lady beetles, ground beetles, earwigs, spiders and dragonflies feed on eggs and larvae, so avoid early spraying. See our guide on [integrated pest management](/pests/integrated-pest-management).

blocks.text: When to Act: the Light Trap and the Egg Jar Test

items.title: Watch the moths
items.text: From panicle initiation on, run a light trap at night and count the stem borer moths it catches. A rising catch tells you that egg laying is under way.

items.title: Collect egg masses
items.text: If the moths are many from booting to flowering, many eggs are likely in the field too. Collect some stem borer egg masses from the leaves, put them in a jar, cover it and wait for them to hatch.

items.title: Read the jar
items.text: If more borer larvae than tiny wasps come out, PhilRice says a contact or stomach insecticide is needed. If the wasps outnumber the larvae, the natural enemies are winning, so hold the spray.

items.title: Help hit plants recover
items.text: After deadhearts, keep the field free of drought stress and weeds. PhilRice also advises adding fertilizer so the crop recovers.

blocks.text: Rice stem borers are best held down by resistant varieties and the steps above. If a spray is truly needed, ask your agricultural technician first, use only a product registered for rice, and never spray in the first 30 to 40 days after transplanting unless the pest is at outbreak level. Early sprays kill spiders and wasps and invite planthopper outbreaks. Let the jar test, not the look of the damage, make that call. Our guide on [when to spray rice pests](/blog/when-to-spray-rice-pests) puts the stem borer next to the other rice pests.

blocks.title: Spray safely
blocks.text: Use only products registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label for the rate, the timing and the protective clothing. Switch to a different insecticide group next time, so the pest does not learn to survive it. Our [guide to integrated pest management](/pests/integrated-pest-management) explains how.

items: Use resistant varieties where your technician can supply them.
Clear stubble, ratoon and volunteer rice right after harvest.
Plant the whole area in the same weeks, and keep a fallow gap between crops.
Scout the seedbed for egg masses before every transplanting.
Keep records of deadhearts and whiteheads by lot, so you see early which fields are repeat targets.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Rice Stem Borer

items.q: What is the difference between a deadheart and a whitehead?
items.a: A deadheart is a dried central tiller before flowering. A whitehead is a white, empty panicle after flowering. Both come from a larva feeding inside the stem.

items.q: Can I see the borer from outside the stem?
items.a: Not usually. Look for tiny holes, then split the stem to find the larva and the frass. The egg masses on the leaves are easier to spot.

items.q: Should I spray as soon as I see deadhearts?
items.a: No. Spraying early kills the spiders and wasps that feed on borers. Handpick egg masses, manage the water, do the egg jar test, and ask a technician before you spray.

items.q: What is the egg jar test for stem borer?
items.a: Collect stem borer egg masses from the field, keep them in a covered jar and let them hatch. If more larvae than wasps come out, PhilRice says a spray is needed. If more wasps come out, the natural enemies have the borer in hand.
